transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-08
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 58 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Li (Redwood AE), Priya Raman (Redwood SE), Carlos Mendez (Redwood Eng), Anya Patel (Redwood Solutions), Evan Shaw (HelixMed ML Infra Lead), Maya Rao (HelixMed Head of ML), Ben Cho (HelixMed Platform Eng), Sofia Kim (HelixMed Security)

Summary: quick technical workshop to triage a post-quantize accuracy regression HelixMed observed on their on-prem cluster. Focus: compare GPTQ vs AWQ vs FP8 per-layer behavior, discuss precision fallback strategies and KV/batching interplay, and agree on bisect plan + next steps.

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan: okay everyone thanks for joining, I know we have a packed agenda. quick intro round then jump straight into the regression notes Evan sent.
[00:07] Evan: yeah thanks, we'll keep it focused. we started seeing a small but material uptick in hallucinations after the last quantize run — roughly 3 to 5% increase on our NER and summarization suites.
[00:18] Maya: and it only happens on our on-prem cluster, not in the dev cloud runs which is weird, same model checkpoint aside from the quantization artifact.
[00:26] Priya: okay, couple of quick clarifiers — when you say "quantize run" you mean you applied our GPTQ pipeline or the AWQ one?
[00:33] Evan: we tried both but primarily the internal team ran a GPTQ flow first; later we attempted AWQ with default layer map, and FP8 experimental. the worst regression was with GPTQ at int8.
[00:42] Carlos: got it. and what's your inference runtime — is this our on-prem package with local Redwood Private runtime or a fork?
[00:48] Ben: we're running Redwood Private 1.13 on a VPC-like network, basically customer-managed. uses RTX A6000-ish nodes, RDMA between hosts, and a custom NFS-mounted KV cache.
[00:57] Anya: custom NFS for KV cache — that rings an alarm bell, the sticky KV semantics differ a lot between local disk and NFS, latency distribution shifts, which can change batching behaviour.
[01:06] Sofia: also note we have FIPS KMS in the loop for keys, not sure if that affects serialization times for checkpoint loads.
[01:12] Priya: thanks — so three likely contributors: 1) quantization algorithm differences (GPTQ vs AWQ vs FP8), 2) KV cache performance differences on NFS/RDMA vs local NVMe, 3) batching policy interacting with per-token latency SLO, which can bias choices leading to early termination or truncation.
[01:25] Jordan: can we walk through a concrete failing example? Evan, do you have a prompt and output?
[01:30] Evan: yes I'll paste in chat — short clinical note -> extract medication list. post-quantize, the model sometimes omits low-frequency drugs and invents dosages.
[01:38] Maya: and these are high-weight signals in our eval; even small precision losses are visible.
[01:42] Priya: understood. my immediate ask is: can you confirm the exact model commit and the quantization config (layer map, per-channel vs per-tensor, symmetric/asymmetric, block size)?
[01:52] Ben: commit is abc1234, GPTQ with per-channel scale, block 128, symmetric. AWQ we ran default 16-block config; FP8 we used dynamic exponent range.
[02:01] Priya: that's helpful. we'll run a layerwise sweep. quick note: GPTQ's 2-pass reconstruction can hurt some low-signal embeddings depending on which layers you quantize; AWQ tends to preserve first and last n layers better by default, but config specifics matter.
[02:14] Carlos: also worth noting runtime fallback options — Redwood runtime supports precision gating per-layer at runtime if you ship a mixed-precision artifact. we can enable a canary that runs the last N layers in FP16 while keeping the rest int8 to see impact.
[02:25] Evan: can we do that without rebuilding the entire model binary?
[02:28] Priya: yes, if you keep the FP16 slice artifacts available the runtime can selectively route the attention/matmul ops of selected layers to the FP16 kernels. that does increase memory but it's a common troubleshooting pattern.
[02:36] Maya: is that the "layer fallback" you mentioned earlier? does it affect KV cache layout?
[02:40] Priya: sticky KV layout remains the same in principle — the cache holds key/value tensors; switching execution precision for a layer changes the memory representation and may need per-layer serialization logic. on local NVMe we saw this transition cost negligible, on NFS it added 20–60 ms per cache load in some tests.
[02:53] Ben: that matches our numbers, and our batching tends to coalesce small requests which amplifies latency jitter.
[03:00] Jordan: okay let's catalogue experiments we need: A) per-layer accuracy sweep (GPTQ vs AWQ vs FP8) B) runtime canary with last-3-layer FP16 fallback C) KV cache locality test (local tmpfs vs NFS) D) batching policy tweak to prefer micro-batches for low-latency NER tasks.
[03:16] Evan: agreed. which of these can Redwood run and which we should run?
[03:20] Priya: Redwood can run A + B on a matched model binary if you share the failing prompts and commit. We can't run C on your on-prem NFS but we can simulate latency profiles. B requires the mixed-precision artifact or we can produce one and ship. D is configuration we can propose and you can test locally.
[03:33] Maya: simulating RDMA latency is helpful but we want real numbers, what's the best way to capture environment traces?
[03:38] Carlos: capture perf traces: token latency distribution, KV cache hit/miss logs, batch size histograms per route, and NIC stats for RDMA rtts. if you can pull a 30-minute trace that includes failing calls that's ideal.
[03:48] Ben: we'll collate that and send.
[03:51] Priya: on the quantization side, quick explanation for the team — GPTQ minimizes reconstruction error for weight matrices by optimizing per-block quantization residuals; it sometimes overfits to high-norm dimensions so rare-token behavior can degrade. AWQ trades slightly higher MSE for better distributional preservation across vectors, often better for generative NER. FP8 has different dynamic range behavior and can be surprisingly good for attention layers but worse in dense MLPs unless calibrated.
[04:16] Sofia: from security perspective, are there any risks with shipping mixed-precision artifacts or having fallback toggles exposed? audit trail concerns.
[04:23] Jordan: good point — Redwood's runtime logs any precision gating switch and stores audit events; we can add an immutable event to your audit log and tie it to SAML identity. we also support HSM-protected artifact signing to prevent tampering.
[04:36] Sofia: ok that sounds fine, we'll want the doc for compliance.
[04:40] Anya: circling back to KV/batching — there's an interaction where larger batches produce fewer KV cache lookups because prefix caching kicks in more, but they also change token interleaving which can expose quantization noise earlier in the decode. So sometimes reducing batch size for sensitive routes improves quality albeit at cost.
[04:55] Maya: we've noticed that in production: our summarization route is batched aggressively and shows higher regression than single-turn NER.
[05:02] Priya: suggested experiment: decouple routes — enforce per-route batching policies so critical tasks use micro-batches (1–4) while cheap ones remain batched. we can give a config diff.
[05:10] Jordan: question for HelixMed — what are your latency SLOs and cost constraints? helps prioritize fallback choices.
[05:15] Evan: SLO is 200ms p95 for NER inference; cost target is sub-$0.004 per 1k tokens on dedicated capacity, but we are flexible if accuracy is impacted.
[05:24] Priya: 200ms p95 is tight on A6000 with int8+NFS; micro-batches will help quality but may risk p95. layer-fallback of last-3 layers to FP16 usually slows tokens by ~10–20% depending on kernel mix.
[05:36] Carlos: if we enable adaptive precision gating (only escalate to FP16 on low-confidence tokens flagged by the softmax entropy), we can get the best of both worlds. cost is the control complexity and you need a short-latency confidence scorer.
[05:47] Maya: do you have that pattern implemented?
[05:49] Priya: we have a reference implementation — it uses a light-weight scorer on the logits before top-k, and if entropy below threshold we re-run last layers at higher precision. we can prototype on your dev cluster.
[05:58] Ben: re-running last layers — does that duplicate KV lookups and blow up latency?
[06:02] Priya: it can, but the scorer often catches <5% of tokens; the incremental latency is bounded. still, on NFS the re-load cost matters. that's why local KV or sticky warming is important.
[06:12] Jordan: action item: Priya will run per-layer sweep and also produce a mixed-precision canary artifact. Evan will share prompts + traces. Jordan to send sticky-KV and VPC docs. agreed?
[06:23] Everyone: yes.
[06:26] [06:26] Priya: technical notes for the sweep: we'll run three families: 1) GPTQ-int8 full quantize, 2) AWQ-int8 with preserved first and last 2 layers, 3) FP8 with calibrated exp range. metrics: EM/F1 for NER, ROUGE for summarization, and perplexity on QA set. We'll produce delta vs baseline fp16.
[06:44] Evan: can you include a per-layer weight perturbation visualization? our data science team finds that helpful.
[06:49] Priya: yes, per-layer delta histograms + scatter plots. we'll push raw CSVs.
[06:53] Carlos: and I will simulate NFS latency profiles locally to estimate cache load penalty — we'll include the 20/50/100ms penalties in the report.
[06:59] Maya: about the AWQ defaults — are there known breakage modes if you leave their block size at 16?
[07:04] Priya: AWQ default often uses smaller blocks which are friendlier to low-frequency tokens but increase footprint. bigger block sizes reduce quant noise at cost of memory. it's a tradeoff.
[07:13] Ben: another item — our CI pipeline auto-applies GPTQ from your open-source toolchain; is there a recommended gating test to prevent regressions hitting prod?
[07:20] Jordan: yes, Redwood suggests a small smoke eval (100 high-signal prompts) plus a lightweight synthetic perturbation test. we can provide a Jenkins/CI snippet.
[07:29] Sofia: and full security review — we need the signed artifacts + SBOM for the mixed-precision build.
[07:34] Jordan: we'll include artifact signing and SBOM.
[07:36] Evan: timeline — how fast can you run the sweeps? we need results before next week.
[07:40] Priya: we'll prioritize. initial sweep within 48 hours, deeper per-layer results and CSV by 2026-05-12.
[07:47] Jordan: let's capture tentative follow-up slot: 2026-05-14 1600 UTC for bisect review.
[07:52] Maya: that works.
[07:54] [07:54] - Quick Q&A and clarifications -
[07:54] Ben: small question on mixed artifact size — how much extra memory for keeping FP16 slice for last-3 layers?
[07:58] Priya: ballpark 10–15% depending on layer sizes, sometimes 25% for models with heavy MLP ratio.
[08:05] Carlos: And about runtime gating flags — do we have safe defaults to avoid noisy toggles?
[08:09] Anya: yes, use a minimum token window (e.g., only allow gating every 8 tokens) and a hysteresis counter to prevent oscillation.
[08:15] Sofia: final ask from compliance: include an itemized list of what logs are recorded when you enable canary fallback.
[08:20] Jordan: will include.
[08:22] Priya: ok I'll recap experiments and owners in the notes.
[08:25] Jordan: thanks everyone — we'll follow up via email with artifacts. meeting adjourned.

End of transcript.
